summary.text: The prime number theorem describes how primes are spread among the positive integers, making precise the idea that primes become less common as numbers get larger.
For large N, the chance that a random integer up to N is prime is very close to 1 / log(N).
It was proved independently in 1896 by Jacques Hadamard and Charles Jean de la Vallée Poussin, using ideas introduced by Bernhard Riemann.

facts.label: Average gap
facts.value: Between consecutive primes among the first N integers, about log(N)

facts.label: Doubling the digits
facts.value: A random number is about half as likely to be prime

facts.label: At 1000 digits
facts.value: About one in 2300 integers is prime

items.prompt: You pick a random number with up to 400 digits, then another with up to 800 digits. How do their chances of being prime compare?

options.label: The longer one is about twice as likely
They are about equally likely
The longer one is about half as likely
The longer one cannot be prime

items.explain: A random integer with at most 2n digits is about half as likely to be prime as one with at most n digits, for large enough n.

items.prompt: A student says the estimate x / log x is off by a huge amount for big x, so the theorem must be false. What is wrong with that?

options.label: The theorem is about the shrinking relative error, not the raw difference
The estimate becomes exact once N passes a million
The raw difference between them is always tiny
The theorem only applies to even numbers, not all integers

items.explain: The theorem says nothing about the difference; it says the relative error of the approximation approaches 0 as the numbers grow.

items.prompt: Primes thin out among bigger numbers. How big is the typical distance between neighbouring primes?

options.label: It stays at about two, however far you count
It shrinks toward one as the numbers get larger
It is random, with no typical size at all
About log(N), where N is the count so far

items.explain: The average gap between consecutive primes among the first N integers is roughly log(N).

items.prompt: What did Riemann's 1859 memoir connect to the distribution of primes?

options.label: The zeros of the extended Riemann zeta function
The last digit of each prime
The number of divisors of each integer
The gaps between perfect squares

items.explain: Riemann showed the distribution of primes is intimately connected with the zeros of the analytically extended zeta function, opening the way for complex analysis.

items.prompt: Chebyshev did not prove the full theorem, but his estimates were strong enough for what guarantee?

options.label: Every prime is followed by another within two
A prime always lies between n and 2n (n ≥ 2)
Every large number is a sum of two primes
No prime ends in an even digit

items.explain: They were enough to prove Bertrand's postulate: there is a prime between n and 2n for any integer n ≥ 2.

items.prompt: What everyday idea does the prime number theorem make precise?

options.label: Primes get rarer as numbers get larger
Primes are evenly spaced along the number line
Primes disappear after some very large size
Primes become more common as numbers grow

items.explain: It formalizes the intuitive idea that primes become less common as they become larger, quantifying the rate.
